title: Search Autocomplete
prompt: As someone types into a search box, show the ten most popular completions for what they have typed so far. Suggestions should reflect what people are actually searching for.

clarify.q: Do suggestions match only the start of the query (prefix), or any word inside it?
clarify.why: Prefix-only lets us precompute an answer per prefix. Matching any word or fixing typos turns this into a search-engine problem with very different indexes.

clarify.q: How fresh must suggestions be? Should a breaking news query show up within minutes?
clarify.why: Daily freshness is a batch job. Minutes means a streaming path for trending queries alongside the batch index.

clarify.q: Are suggestions personalised, localised, or the same for everyone?
clarify.why: Global suggestions can be cached at a CDN and shared by millions. Per-user results cannot, which moves load from the edge to our servers.

clarify.q: How many suggestions, and how many languages?
clarify.why: Ten per prefix sets the entry size. Several languages and scripts change tokenisation and multiply the index per locale.
Offensive terms, personal data people typed (phone numbers, names), and legally sensitive items need a filter and a minimum popularity threshold.

clarify.q: What is the latency target from keystroke to suggestions on screen?
clarify.why: Under about 100 ms feels instant. That sets the server budget to tens of milliseconds and pushes us toward in-memory lookups and edge caching.

functional: Given a prefix of 1 to 30 characters, return up to 10 completions ranked by popularity.
Rankings are built from real query logs and favour recent popularity.
Trending queries can appear within about 15 minutes.
Blocked and low-popularity queries are never suggested.
Results are per locale (language and country).
nonFunctional: Server p99 under 20 ms; end-to-end under 100 ms on a good connection.
Availability 99.99%; if suggestions fail the search box still works.
Eventual consistency: suggestion lists may lag the logs by minutes to a day.
outOfScope: Running the actual search after the user presses enter.
The frontend dropdown component in detail.

assumptions: 100 M daily active users, 5 searches each per day
About 6 suggestion requests per search after client debounce
20 M distinct queries pass the popularity and safety filter
Average suggestible query about 20 characters; only index prefixes up to 15 characters
Each prefix entry stores 10 query ids plus key: about 100 B

steps.label: Suggestion requests
steps.result: ≈ 35 k/s average, ~100 k/s at a 3× peak

steps.label: Search log volume
steps.result: ≈ 50 GB of logs per day to aggregate

steps.label: Prefix entries (upper bound)
steps.math: 20 M queries × 15 prefixes = 300 M entries, before sharing common prefixes

steps.label: Index size (upper bound)
steps.math: 300 M × 100 B = 30 GB; plus query strings 20 M × 30 B = 0.6 GB
steps.result: ≤ 31 GB: fits in RAM on one large machine

steps.label: Replicas needed
steps.math: 100 k/s peak ÷ ~20 k lookups/s per node (with headroom) = 5; add zones and spare
steps.result: ≈ 8 to 10 full replicas per region, no sharding

estimates.takeaway: The whole index fits in memory on one machine, so replicate, do not shard. Every node holds the full map and any node can answer any prefix. The read rate is high but each lookup is a hash get. Short prefixes are shared by everyone, so an edge cache absorbs a big share before traffic reaches us. The real work is the offline pipeline that turns 50 GB of logs a day into that index.

api.note: Cache-Control: public, max-age=300 for global results; the prefix is normalised (lowercase, trimmed) before lookup.
Emitted by the search service, not the suggest service.
Builder publishes a new immutable snapshot; serving nodes load it and swap atomically.
Takes effect immediately as a serving-time filter, then in the next build.

entities.name: PrefixIndex
entities.store: In-memory hash map on every serving node, loaded from a snapshot file
fields: ids into the query table, best first
entities.why: One hash lookup per request. Built offline, immutable while serving.

entities.name: QueryTable
entities.store: Same snapshot, array indexed by query id
entities.why: Prefix entries hold ids, not strings, so each query string is stored once.

entities.name: QueryCounts
entities.store: Columnar files in object storage (daily partitions)
entities.why: Output of daily aggregation; the builder reads the last 30 days to compute decayed scores.

entities.name: TrendingOverlay
entities.store: Small in-memory map pushed every 5 min
entities.why: Lets fast-rising queries appear between daily builds.

data.note: We precompute the answer for every prefix instead of walking a trie at request time, so serving is a single hash lookup. Snapshots are versioned files: a bad build is rolled back by pointing nodes at the previous version. Distinct-user counts, not raw counts, decide what is eligible, so one bot repeating a query cannot get it suggested.

hld.summary:
Two halves. The offline path collects search events into a log stream, a daily job aggregates them into counts per query and locale, and an index builder applies time decay, filters (blocklist, minimum distinct users), computes the top 10 for every prefix, and writes an immutable snapshot to object storage. A streaming job watches the last hour for spikes and publishes a small trending overlay every 5 minutes.

The online path is simple: the client debounces keystrokes, the request hits a CDN that caches global results for a few minutes, misses go to stateless suggest servers that hold the full index in memory, merge the trending overlay, apply the live blocklist and return.

diagram.title: Offline build and online serving

flows.title: Typing 'new yo'
steps: Client waits 100 ms after the last keystroke, cancels any in-flight request, sends /v1/suggest?q=new yo.
CDN has the key cached from someone else's request a minute ago and returns it in ~10 ms.
On a miss, a suggest server normalises the prefix, does one hash lookup, maps ids to strings.
It merges any trending boosts for that prefix, drops anything matching the live blocklist, returns 10 items.

flows.title: Daily rebuild
steps: Aggregation job counts yesterday's 500 M searches by normalised query and locale.
Builder reads 30 days of counts and computes score = sum of count × 0.9^ageInDays.
It drops queries with fewer than 50 distinct users or matching the blocklist.
For each query, for each of its prefixes up to 15 chars, it keeps a running top 10, then writes the snapshot.
Serving nodes download the snapshot, load it beside the old one, and swap a pointer; canary nodes first.

flows.title: A trending query appears
steps: Streaming job counts queries in 5-minute windows and compares with the same window last week.
A query whose rate jumps more than 10× and passes the distinct-user and safety filters gets a boost.
The overlay is pushed to all suggest servers; the CDN TTL of 5 minutes bounds how long old answers live.

deepDives.title: Which data structure serves a prefix?
deepDives.problem: For any prefix we need the 10 best completions in a few milliseconds. Scanning all queries that start with 'a' at request time is far too slow; the question is how much to precompute.

options.name: Trie walked at request time
options.how: Build a trie of queries; on request, walk to the prefix node and search the subtree for the top 10.
cons: Subtree search for a short prefix touches millions of nodes
Pointer-heavy structure is cache-unfriendly

options.name: Trie with top 10 cached at every node
options.how: Same trie, but each node stores the ids of its best 10 completions, computed at build time.
pros: Lookup is a walk of at most 15 nodes
cons: Still pointer chasing; harder to serialise and load fast
Updating one count means fixing ancestors

options.name: Flat prefix-to-top-10 map
options.how: Precompute a hash map from each prefix string to 10 query ids. The builder does all the work.
pros: Easy to snapshot, load and swap
Trivial to cache at a CDN by key
cons: Stores each prefix key in full, so larger than a trie
Any change needs a rebuild or an overlay

options.name: Search engine completion feature
options.how: Use an engine like Elasticsearch with edge n-grams or a completion field.
pros: Fuzzy matching and filters for free
cons: A cluster to run for what is a lookup table
Higher and less predictable latency

deepDives.choice: Flat map, because the upper-bound estimate is about 30 GB, which fits in RAM, and it makes the serving code almost nothing. Long prefixes beyond 15 characters fall back to the 15-character entry filtered by the full prefix. If we needed fuzzy matching or in-word matches across hundreds of millions of queries, or the index grew past a single machine's memory, I would move to a trie with cached top-k sharded by first characters, or to a search engine.

deepDives.title: Turning query logs into rankings
deepDives.problem: Popularity changes. A query that was huge last year should fade, and seasonal terms should rise. Bots and single users repeating a query should not move rankings. Processing 50 GB a day must be cheap and repeatable.

options.name: All-time counts
options.how: Keep adding to a total count per query since launch.
cons: Old queries never fade
New queries can never catch up

options.name: Sliding window, last N days
options.how: Score is the count over the last 30 days.
cons: Sharp cliff when a day drops out
Treats 29 days ago the same as yesterday

options.name: Exponential time decay
options.how: Score is the sum of daily counts times 0.9 to the power of the day's age, recomputed daily.
cons: Still slow for news-speed trends
Decay factor needs tuning per locale

deepDives.choice: Exponential decay in the daily batch, counting distinct users per query per day rather than raw hits so a bot cannot pump one query. With 0.9 per day, a day's searches lose half their weight in about 6.6 days (0.9^6.6 ≈ 0.5). Add the streaming trending overlay for news-speed changes. If the product were a store catalogue search where popularity is stable, a weekly batch alone would do.

deepDives.title: Hitting the latency budget
deepDives.problem: The user types fast. Each keystroke could fire a request; responses can arrive out of order; and 100 k requests/s is a lot of servers if every one of them reaches us.

options.name: Request every keystroke, no caching
options.how: Fire a request per character and render whatever comes back.
cons: Wasted requests for characters typed in quick succession
Out-of-order responses flash stale suggestions

options.name: Client debounce, cancel and local cache
options.how: Wait ~100 ms of idle, abort the previous request, keep a small map of prefix to results for the session.
pros: Cuts requests by more than half
Backspace is instant from the local cache
cons: Adds up to 100 ms on purpose
Needs care to ignore late responses

options.name: CDN caching of responses
options.how: Global, non-personal results get Cache-Control with a few minutes TTL, keyed by normalised prefix and locale.
pros: Short prefixes are shared by everyone, so the hit rate is high
cons: Up to TTL minutes stale
Cannot cache personalised results

deepDives.choice: All three of the cheap ones: debounce, cancel and session cache on the client, plus a 5-minute CDN TTL. Our own servers then see mostly the long-tail prefixes, and each is one in-memory lookup well under 1 ms of CPU. If we added personalisation, the CDN would cache the global list and the client would blend a small personal list (recent searches) locally.

deepDives.title: What must never be suggested
deepDives.problem: Suggestions are our words in the user's search box. A slur, a private phone number someone searched, or a defamatory phrase becomes our responsibility the moment we show it.

options.name: Filter only in the builder
options.how: Drop blocked queries when building the snapshot.
cons: A newly reported query stays visible until the next build

options.name: Builder filter plus live serving filter
options.how: Builder excludes known bad items; servers also check a small live blocklist pushed within a minute.
cons: Live list must stay small and fast to match
CDN entries still need purging

deepDives.choice: Both, plus a privacy floor: a query is eligible only if at least 50 distinct users searched it, which keeps one-off personal data out. A takedown updates the live blocklist and issues a CDN purge for the affected prefixes. If the product were an internal tool with trusted users, the builder filter would be enough.

failures: A bad snapshot ships (empty or full of junk)
Builder validates size and samples against the previous version; canary nodes first; roll back by pointing to the previous snapshot.
The log pipeline stalls for a day
Keep serving yesterday's snapshot; suggestions are slightly stale but correct.
A suggest node runs out of memory during a swap
Size nodes for two snapshots at once, or load into a fresh process and switch traffic.
A bot farm tries to push a query into suggestions
Count distinct users, rate-limit search per user, and require the trend to hold over several windows.
Purge affected prefix keys on takedown; keep TTL short (5 minutes).
scale: 10× queries in the index (200 M): the upper bound grows to about 300 GB, so shard the map by prefix hash or first two characters, with a thin router; or switch to a trie per shard to share prefixes.
Many locales: one snapshot per locale; small locales share nodes, big ones get dedicated replicas.
Personalisation: keep the global index as is and add a per-user recent-searches list on the client or a small per-user store, blended at the edge.

followups.q: How would you add typo tolerance?
answer: Generate likely corrections for the prefix with an edit-distance index over popular queries, only after the exact prefix returns too few results.
Or precompute common misspellings to their correct form in the builder.

followups.q: Why not update the index on every search event?
answer: Writes would hit every replica 5 800 times a second and fight with reads.
Rankings barely change minute to minute except for trends, which the overlay handles.
Immutable snapshots are easy to test and roll back.

followups.q: How do you decide the CDN TTL?
answer: Trade freshness against hit rate; 5 minutes matches the trending overlay cadence.
Short prefixes could get longer TTLs because they change least.

followups.q: How do you measure whether suggestions are good?
answer: Track the share of searches that came from a suggestion and the position clicked.
A/B test decay factors and thresholds.

mistakes: Walking a trie and searching subtrees at request time instead of precomputing top results.
Sharding a 30 GB index that fits on one machine instead of replicating it.
Counting raw hits so a bot can push a query into everyone's suggestions.
Forgetting client debounce and request cancellation, then sizing for a request per keystroke.
No plan for removing an offensive suggestion quickly.
